title: My dev tips from making my first game in 4 months with Claude Code (2.3 Billion is out on Steam)
author: Guilty_Butterfly_921
selftext:
**About the game:** 2.3 Billion is a short active incremental: you play every lap yourself, with a controller or a keyboard, and every perk changes how you play. A few hours long, $2.99. I'm solo.

# How I work with the AI

I keep the design and the feel for myself: the controller feel, the mechanics and their combinations, the UI/UX, the sounds and the VFX. I don't find writing code especially fun, so I delegate it, but my experience as an app developer helps me know what to ask for.

* One model per task: Opus for the game code, Sonnet for small edits, Fable for long investigations like a performance drop with no known cause.
* Claude writes automated tests along with the code, and a bot plays real laps of the game to measure how strong each perk build is. But a bot has blind spots, so playtests are still necessary: judging and adjusting, again and again.
* Be suspicious: AI can be wrong with a lot of confidence, even the smartest models out there (Fable 5.2 today).

I started with Antigravity and Gemini 3.1 Pro, then switched to Claude Code for the code: a much more complete interface, and models that handled my problems better. Engine: Godot 4.

# The tip that helped me a lot: a marker key for playtests

I asked Claude to add a key to the game: when I press M while playing, everything freezes and a box opens where I write what I just felt. Claude also built a telemetry tool made for my game, which writes a timeline of the whole session, and each note lands on it at the exact moment, with where I was and the time left in the lap.

So instead of "the middle feels slow", Claude gets the exact point of the run and what was happening, and can check it against the numbers. (Only in my playtest builds: the released game records nothing.)

# The oldest tip, still true: scope it so you can finish

I tried making games earlier in my life, and overscoping is partly why I gave up. So I picked the incremental genre: it's systems more than content, which is straightforward enough to code with AI.

I'm not an illustrator, so everything is drawn by code, and the ambiance is abstract on purpose: for a small project, I think it's the simplest to do. For the sounds, every one is made by me in Logic Pro, with what I've learned from YouTube videos and Gemini.

# Numbers

* First commit on August 8, so about 4 months of work
* 64 wishlists at release, 72 now
* 29 copies sold since November 27 (2 refunded)

I know it won't pay back what I put into it, but it's the price of learning, and I'll do better on the next one.

The marker key comes from my experience as a project manager. I'd like to share more with people who build games, so I'd be happy to talk about it in the comments.

Thanks for reading, I hope it helps!

[**2.3 Billion on Steam**](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5412670/)
